```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
library(jcglasso)
```

## 1. The model

For each of `K` sub-populations (classes), the `q` predictors follow a Gaussian
graphical model, $X_k \sim N(\mu_k, \Omega_k^{-1})$, and the `p` responses follow
a conditional Gaussian graphical model,
$Y_k \mid X_k = x \sim N(\beta_{0k} + B_k^\top x, \Theta_k^{-1})$.
Responses and predictors can be censored (with known limits) or missing at
random. The joint conditional graphical lasso (Sottile et al., 2025) maximizes the
observed log-likelihood penalized by sparse group lasso penalties on
$\{B_k\}$, $\{\Theta_k\}$ and $\{\Omega_k\}$, with tuning parameters
$\lambda$, $\rho$ and $\nu$ and mixing parameters $\alpha_2$, $\alpha_1$ and
$\alpha_3$ (lasso for $\alpha = 1$, group lasso for $\alpha = 0$).

## 2. Data

`rjcggm()` simulates data as in the simulation study of the paper: right-censored
responses and missing values in responses and predictors.

```{r data}
set.seed(1234)
sim <- rjcggm(n = 100, p = 10, q = 4, K = 2, ncompPrecision = 2, ncompB = 2)
sim$Z
summary(sim$Z)$class1
```

`datajcggm()` creates the same kind of object from a list of matrices of
responses (and predictors), with censoring limits `lo` and `up` and `NA` for the
missing values.

## 3. Selection of the tuning parameters

Following Section 6 of the paper, $\nu$ is first selected on the model of the
predictors alone (`sim$ZX` contains the predictors as responses) with the BIC
computed from the Q-function:

```{r nu}
fitx <- jcglasso(data = sim$ZX, nrho = 10, rho.min.ratio = 0.1)
bicx <- BIC(fitx)
plot(bicx)
nu <- select_jcglasso(fitx, GoF = bicx)$rho
nu
```

Then $\lambda$ and $\rho$ are selected on a two-dimensional grid, with $\nu$
fixed:

```{r fit}
fit <- jcglasso(data = sim$Z, nrho = 5, rho.min.ratio = 0.1, nlambda = 5,
                lambda.min.ratio = 0.1, nu = nu)
fit
bic <- BIC(fit)
plot(bic)
best <- select_jcglasso(fit, GoF = bic)
```

The optimality conditions of the M-step can be checked at the selected model:

```{r kkt}
kkt(best)
```

## 4. Maximum likelihood refit and estimates

```{r mle}
mle <- jcggm(best)
round(coef(mle, type = "B", class.id = 1), 2)
plot(mle, "Theta")
```

`impute()`, `fitted()` and `residuals()` give the imputed data (conditional
expected values of the censored and missing values), the fitted values and the
residuals.

```{r impute}
head(impute(mle)$class1[, 1:5])
```

## 5. Graphs

With package 'igraph', `to_graph()` returns the estimated graphs of each class.

```{r graphs, eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
gr <- to_graph(mle)
gr
plot(gr, type = "conditional")
```

## 6. Computational notes

* The EM algorithm alternates an E-step (conditional expected values of the
  sufficient statistics, with the approximation of Guo et al. (2015) for the second
  moments of censored values) and an M-step in which $\Omega$ is updated by the
  joint graphical lasso, $B$ by an accelerated proximal gradient (APG) algorithm
  and $\Theta$ by the joint graphical lasso.
* The joint graphical lasso (ADMM of Danaher et al., 2014) is applied separately
  to the connected components identified by the screening rule; isolated
  variables have closed-form estimates.
* For the regression coefficients, APG was compared with the ADMM described in
  the paper (with penalty parameter $\tau = 2$) on simulated problems: both reach
  the same solution, APG with 2-4 times fewer iterations and less computing time,
  also with highly correlated responses.
* The path is computed with warm starts; only the estimates, the values of the
  Q-function and the degrees of freedom are stored.

## References

Sottile, G., Augugliaro, L., Vinciotti, V., Arancio, W. and Coronnello, C. (2025).
Sparse inference of the human haematopoietic system from heterogeneous and
partially observed genomic data. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series
C: Applied Statistics*, 74(1), 204-228.

Danaher, P., Wang, P. and Witten, D. M. (2014). The joint graphical lasso for
inverse covariance estimation across multiple classes. *Journal of the Royal
Statistical Society Series B*, 76(2), 373-397.

Guo, J., Levina, E., Michailidis, G. and Zhu, J. (2015). Graphical models for
ordinal data. *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*, 24(1), 183-204.
